The h2 exchange is part of a larger forced queen attack. The non-taking search has Ne3 and wins by checks, with no verified need to stop that pawn by giving up the rook.
After Be7 the king and d-pawn advance together. Bxd2 loses the bishop and declining via g4 or Kg5 allows d1=Q.
After Kg7 and Ke7, taking the d-pawn loses a rook; attempting Rf8 allows d8=Q and another rook trade. Bxd7 instead trades a bishop for the pawn and enables rook checks.
Rf2 allows Kd6 and the rook must be given for the g-pawn. The non-taking line after g5 reaches the same sacrifice later. Rc1 activates the rook.
The root loses a rook before the pawn advances and the analysed first replies diverge. The c-pawn conversion contributes, but the distinct cost of stopping it is uncertain.

After Bb2 Qc2 Rc1 d2, Qxd2 Qxd2 Rxc8 leaves queen for rook and pawn. Declining with b4 permits d1=Q. Bd2 avoids this liquidation.
Stronger branches have their own d2 sacrifices with different checks and material compensation; the root contrast involves more than the local interception.
Both choices can lead to Bxe2 Rxe2. The played move changes the timing and counterplay, beyond this exact interception label.
g2+ forces Rxg2, which is answered by Rxg2. Rg2 changes the placement before the pawn check and avoids this loss in the stronger branches.
The h-pawn forces Rook for pawn after Ra5, and the independent non-taking option permits h1=Q. Ra1 leaves a different checking route before the h-pawn can advance.

After Kf4 Kf2 the rook is lost on g2; avoiding it allows g1=Q and Rxg1 Kxg1. Kd2 supplies repeated checks.
The non-taking line wins the bishop on f3 instead. Whether the passed pawn itself forces that loss is unclear.
Nf4 permits e2 Nxe2 Qxe2 while Qc5 allows exf1=Q+. Qxe3 removes the original runner earlier.
Rc1 allows the pawn on g2 to win a rook after Rh1; removing the supporting rook instead allows gxh1=Q+. Rb1 avoids both.
Both Kf4 and Kf3 lose the rook on b2. The following knight and king play changes the evaluation.
hxg5 gives the a-pawn a race it wins. Bxa2 Nxa2 costs a bishop; declining permits a1=Q. Bxa4 takes that pawn before it advances.
After Bd1 the e-pawn advances to e2. Bxe2 is met by fxe2, losing the bishop while the replacement pawn can promote. The independent alternative allows the original e-pawn to promote.
Rc2 Rb2 Re2 c2 costs a rook on c2, including after deferring with Rc5. Ke3 maintains central counterplay and avoids this pawn liquidation.
After e7, deeper lines include costly captures of the same d2 pawn. Rxd2 Bxd2 also occurs after a delay. Nb3 gives Nxd2 without a loss.
The same d2 pawn costs a rook in both branches. The stronger defends by other resources.
The stronger line can also sacrifice on f2, with a different role and compensation. The poorer line shares the interception but the change in queen and rook coordination is intertwined.
Both choices give up material on b2. The new interceptor and queen-sacrifice alternatives need a separate comparative evaluation.
Ng5+ Ke7 Rxd2 gives up a rook, with the knight compensation still leaving a material loss. Rd5 delays the same exchange. Nxd2 avoids this initially.
Ke2 Re4+ Kf3 Re1 makes the d2 pawn costly to capture. Rxc6+ delays the same sacrifice rather than resolving the pawn, while Rxc6+ at the root avoids it.
Both choices lose a bishop stopping the same pawn; rook activity and which recapture occurs alter the consequence.
Re2 permits g2 Rxg2 Kxg2. Rf2 instead allows g1=Q. Rxg3+ removes the original pawn before it can advance.
Kg4 Rh7 forces a rook trade for the h-pawn or lets it promote after Rd3. g6 permits a better rook defence.
Rb2 d2 leaves Rxd2 answered by Rxd2+, while Rc2 allows the rook decoy Ra1+ and promotion. Rc3 d2 Rd3 prevents that cost.
Rb7 Rxh7 produces a costly Rxb2 Kxb2; the non-taking continuation also reaches it. Rc7+ preserves checking resources and avoids the same cost.
Kg5 lets the king support the d-pawn advance. Taking it costs a bishop in the independent reply, while the paired reply and restricted defence show it promoting. Kg3 allows Kxd3.
The stronger pair sometimes concedes the same intercepted pawn and the independent stronger reply can avoid it. The root difference is not isolated.
The costly interception is clear, but declining loses to an adjacent passer's promotion. Attribution to the original pawn alone is uncertain.
Both branches concede material against a passed d-pawn. The original and replacement pawns jointly constrain the defence.
After Qxg6+, d2 is protected and Bxd2 gives up a bishop; the restricted Kg2 instead permits promotion. The root Nd4+ lets Bxd2 take without this cost.

Rxa7 permits a connected passer tactic. Rxc2 dxc2+ Kxc2 costs a rook for two pawns. Choosing Ke1 allows the original pawn to promote on c1.
Kg3 allows Kd4 and Bd3, leading to Rxc2 Bxc2 or a c-pawn promotion if play continues on the h-file. Rc5+ creates materially different counterplay.

Kf1 lets the defended d2-pawn take a rook through the Rxd2 exchange. The non-taking line delays its promotion. Qh5 instead can take back the promoted piece economically.
Both root choices pay a comparable minor-piece material cost on f2.

Ne3 leads to c2 and exchanges that convert the original c-pawn and adjacent d-pawn. The opposite move does not concede that sequence. Taking later can cost either minor; skipping the immediate capture lets c1=Q+.
